155.title: The moon's two halves
155.hook: the moon cursed to waste away and given back half of every month; why Hindu holy days move with it
155.carry: holy days follow the moon, and come round again
155.howItsDone: Most Hindu festivals are set by a lunar day, a tithi, in the bright or dark half of a lunar month, so families find each year's dates in a panchang, a printed almanac or app; the waxing and waning moon is told in the story of Daksha's curse on Chandra, softened by Shiva at Prabhasa (Somnath).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Onam: King Bali, who gave himself and still comes home once a year. Your line was bali gave himself: the highest offering. Today, why every one of these festivals moves, and a story about the moon.

Here's a question Hindu kids get asked at school every year: why is Diwali on a different date this time? Holi, Janmashtami, Ganesh Chaturthi, nearly every festival of the last two and a half weeks wanders around the wall calendar. The answer is the moon. And Hindus tell a story about why the moon grows and shrinks at all.
screen: `WHY DID DIWALI MOVE?` → `EVERY FESTIVAL WANDERS.` → `THE ANSWER IS THE MOON.`

segments.voice: The sage Daksha had many daughters, and twenty-seven of them married the Moon, Chandra. Each wife was a star, one of the twenty-seven the moon passes through each month. But Chandra loved only Rohini, and spent every night with her. The others went home to their father in tears. Daksha warned him: treat them all alike. Chandra didn't change, so Daksha cursed him to waste away. Night by night the moon grew thinner, and the plants he cared for began to fail. In one well-loved telling, Chandra went to the shore at Prabhasa, in Gujarat, and prayed to Shiva, and Shiva softened the curse: the moon would fade for half of every month and grow back for the other half. Pilgrims still go to the temple there, Somnath, lord of the moon. Here's what that means at home. A Hindu month really is counted in those two halves: the bright half, as the moon grows, and the dark half, as it shrinks. Each lunar day is a tithi. Diwali falls on a new moon. Ganesh Chaturthi, on the fourth day of the bright half. So the festivals ride the moon and drift across a sun calendar. To find them, families use a panchang, an almanac of five limbs: the lunar day, the weekday, the star the moon is passing, and two more ways of dividing time. And because the moon always comes back, so do the holy days. Nobody keeps them all; families keep what their region and parents keep. Missed one this year? The moon is already on its way round.
screen: `TWENTY-SEVEN STARS. ONE FAVORITE.` · `A CURSE, SOFTENED: HALF DARK, HALF BRIGHT.` · `THE MONTH IN TWO HALVES.` · `A PANCHANG: THE FIVE LIMBS.` · then, large: `THE HOLY DAYS COME ROUND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Tonight, if you can, find the moon. Is it growing or shrinking: the bright half, or the dark? On some fast nights, many Hindus offer a little water toward the rising moon before they eat. If you pray, fold your hands and greet it; if you don't, just look. Then name one festival you'd like to keep this coming year, and say it to the moon: see you when you come round again.

156.title: Archery in the dark
156.hook: a lamp blows out at dinner, a boy's hand still finds his mouth, and Arjuna learns what practice is
156.carry: abhyasa: practice, repeated, steadies the mind
156.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a small daily round, a morning lamp or prayer, japa on a mala, an evening arti, and add weekly observances and the family's festivals; the Gita (6.35) names abhyasa, repeated practice, with letting go, as what steadies the restless mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, panchang: the moon's two halves, and holy days that come round again. Today, the last day of camp three, and a boy eating dinner in the dark.

Sixty days ago this camp began with the breath you already have. Since then: a mantra, a shelf with a lamp and a flower, a flame at sunset, a way into the temple, a year of festivals. Lovely pieces. But how does anyone keep them going, on a tired Tuesday, for years? The old stories answer with a boy, a bow, and a lamp that blew out.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS OF PIECES.` → `HOW DOES ANYONE KEEP IT UP?` → `A BOY, A BOW, A LAMP BLOWN OUT.`

segments.voice: When the Pandava princes were boys, they learned archery from their teacher, Drona. One night, the story goes, Arjuna was eating dinner when a gust of wind blew out the lamp. In the pitch dark he kept eating, and noticed something: his hand still found his mouth, every time, without looking. It knew the way because it had done it so often. So that's what practice does, he thought. He took his bow out into the night and began to shoot in the dark. Drona heard the bowstring, came out, held him, and promised to make him an archer without equal. Years later, the same Arjuna tells Krishna, in the Gita, that the mind is restless, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. He says the mind is held by two things: abhyasa, practice, repeated, and vairagya, letting go. That's why Hindu practice is daily. A lamp lit every morning. A name said on a mala, around and around. Arti at sunset, the same song. It isn't that once doesn't count. It's that repetition trains the mind the way the dark trained Arjuna's hand, until the practice holds you on the days you can't hold it. So camp three closes by setting your table: one thing for the morning, a breath, a mantra or a lamp; one for sunset, a flame or just facing the light; one for the week, a temple visit or a small fast; and your festivals for the year. Small enough to do in the dark. Tomorrow, camp four: the Gita, in order.

segments.voice: Choose your four pieces. For the morning, one thing you could do tomorrow before your phone: a slow breath, one round of your mantra, or one lamp. For sunset, a flame, or just turning toward the light. For the week, a temple visit, a small fast, or sun salutations on Sunday. For the year, your festivals. Now picture doing the morning one half asleep, without thinking, the way Arjuna's hand found its way in the dark. That's where abhyasa is taking you.

157.title: The field of dharma
157.hook: a blind king asks what happened on the field, and a man with borrowed sight begins to tell him
157.carry: every life is a field of dharma
157.howItsDone: Many Hindus read or chant the Bhagavad Gita at home or in study groups, often a chapter at a time; the whole text is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra, and chapter one opens on the field of Kurukshetra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: Arjuna practicing in the dark, and a practice small enough to survive a Tuesday. Today, a new camp, and a book.

The Bhagavad Gita's first voice isn't Krishna's or Arjuna's. It's an old blind king, far from the battle, asking a question. In Edwin Arnold's translation from 1885: "Ranged thus for battle on the sacred plain— On Kurukshetra—say, Sanjaya! say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?" Camp four is that book, the Song of the Lord, read in order over eleven weeks. Eighteen chapters; tradition counts seven hundred verses. You met its people in the stories: the Pandava brothers, their cousins the Kauravas, Krishna taking the reins of Arjuna's chariot on the eve of war. The Gita begins right there.
screen: `A BLIND KING ASKS.` → `WHAT WROUGHT MY PEOPLE?` → `CAMP FOUR: ONE BOOK, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: The king is Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas. He can't see, and he isn't on the field. The sage Vyasa has given his minister, Sanjaya, the sight to see the whole battle from the palace. So the entire Gita is a report, told to a blind father who already fears the answer. His first words: Dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight. Two names at once: a real place, Kurukshetra, north of Delhi, where pilgrims still go, and dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. Dharma is one of Hinduism's biggest words: what's right, the duty that's yours, the order that holds the world together. And listen to how the king asks: what did my sons do, and Pandu's? Mine, and theirs. Many teachers hear his real blindness there. Sanjaya begins. Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, walks up to his old teacher Drona and lists warriors, ours and theirs, a little too fast. Then old Bhishma, the great-uncle, roars like a lion to cheer him and blows his conch shell. The whole field answers: conches, drums, horns, all at once. On the other side, in a great chariot yoked to white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow theirs. Krishna's is Panchajanya. Arjuna's, Devadatta. Gandhi and many others have read that field as a human life: every life is a field of dharma, where you have to choose what's right while the noise is deafening and nobody has moved yet.
screen: `A REPORT TO A BLIND FATHER.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `MINE, AND THEIRS.` · `THE CONCHES ROAR.` · then, large: `EVERY LIFE IS A FIELD OF DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Picture a wide plain at dawn, lined up with the things you're facing right now: a decision, a person, a deadline, a fear. Let the noise come, the conches and drums and every voice in your head at once, and don't fight it; just hear it. Underneath, notice your breath, still going, steady, like Sanjaya quietly telling what he sees: nobody has to move yet.
The armies. Two sides of one family, lined up on Kurukshetra, the field of dharma, and a roar of conch shells before anyone moves.

158.title: Arjuna asks to see
158.hook: the greatest archer asks for his chariot between the armies, to get a good look at the enemy, and Krishna parks it in front of his grandfather
158.carry: the charioteer showed him: the enemy is family
158.howItsDone: Readers of the Gita often pause on 1.21–1.27, where Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot between the armies and stops before Bhishma and Drona; some readers hear Krishna's first words, telling Arjuna to look, as the quiet start of all that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the armies: a blind king asking, conch shells roaring. Your line was every life is a field of dharma. Today, Arjuna asks for one thing, and gets it.

The conches have finished roaring. Arrows are about to fly. Arjuna, the archer, lifts his bow. Over his chariot flies his banner, and on it is Hanuman, the monkey who carried a mountain, the one you met on this path. Arjuna turns to his driver, Krishna, with a perfectly sensible request: drive me out between the two armies, so I can see who I'm fighting. Any good commander would do it. Size up the other side. Krishna says nothing. He just drives.
screen: `HANUMAN ON THE BANNER.` → `DRIVE ME OUT BETWEEN THEM.` → `KRISHNA JUST DRIVES.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, Arjuna's request is: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me 'chyuta. Between both armies, set my chariot, Achyuta, unfailing one. He wants to see, he says, those who've come to fight for Duryodhana. He's thinking of enemies. Now watch where Krishna stops. Sanjaya tells the king: Krishna drove between the armies and set the chariot down right in front of Bhishma and Drona. Bhishma, the great-uncle Arjuna grew up calling grandfather. Drona, the teacher who taught him to shoot. Of all the places on that huge field, Krishna parks there. And he says one line, his first words in the whole Gita: Partha, look at these Kurus, gathered together. Arjuna looks. The text slows down and lists what he sees, one by one: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law. Every one of them is family, or nearly. He asked to see the enemy, and he saw his people. The verse says he was overcome with pity, and he began to speak, in sorrow. Krishna doesn't argue, warn or explain. He just puts Arjuna where he'll have to see the truth. Hindus love this picture: Krishna as Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer, and many homes and temples show it. Arjuna holds the bow; God holds the reins. A fight looks easy from a distance, where the other side is a category: them. Stop in front of real faces, and the category falls apart. Everything the Gita says next starts here.

Picture Krishna driving your chariot out and stopping right in front of their face, and wonder who raised them, who they're a father, a sister, a grandchild to, what they looked like at ten. You don't have to agree with them; just look, and let them be a person for a minute.

159.title: Arjuna's honest objection
159.hook: his legs give way, his mouth goes dry, the bow slips, and the greatest warrior alive makes his case against the war
159.carry: doubt gets heard in full before it's answered
159.howItsDone: Commentators on the Gita treat Arjuna's objection in 1.28–1.39 as a serious moral argument, and many readers see in it their own moments of doubt before a hard duty; the rest of the Gita is Krishna's answer to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna asked to see, and Achyuta, the unfailing one, stopped the chariot before his grandfather and teacher. Your line was the charioteer showed him: the enemy is family. Today, what Arjuna says when he's done looking.

Think about the last time your body knew before you did. A phone call you didn't want to make, and your hands went cold. A room you didn't want to walk into, and your stomach turned. Arjuna has just looked at his whole family lined up to fight him, and before he can make a single argument, his body makes it for him. His legs give way. His mouth dries up. He's shaking. The hair on his arms stands up. His skin burns. Gandiva, the famous bow, starts slipping from his hand. He can't stand. Then the words come.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS FIRST.` → `LEGS GIVE WAY, MOUTH GOES DRY.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Chapter one, verses twenty-eight to thirty-nine, is Arjuna's objection, and the Gita takes it seriously. Is it cowardice? Many readers hear conscience. The heart of it, in Sanskrit: na cha shreyo 'nupashyami hatva svajanam ahave. I see no good in killing my own people in battle. Then further: na kankshe vijayam Krishna, na cha rajyam sukhani cha. I don't want victory, Krishna, or a kingdom, or pleasures. What would a kingdom be for, he asks, if the people we wanted it for are lying dead on this field? Even if they kill me, he says, I don't want to kill them, not for all three worlds, let alone this earth. Then his sharpest point. Yes, the Kauravas are in the wrong; greed clouds their minds, and they can't see the evil of destroying a family. But we can, he says. Why shouldn't we, who see clearly, turn back? And the Gita gives Arjuna twelve verses to make his case, fully, in his own words, before anyone answers. Krishna doesn't interrupt. When he answers, in the next chapter, his first words are blunt: he calls this a weakness of the heart. Commentators have argued ever since over whether it's conscience or confusion. Either way, it's built into Hinduism's best-loved book: the Gita is a dialogue, and doubt gets the first word. The answer takes the rest of the book. A good teacher lets you say the whole thing.
screen: `COWARDICE, OR CONSCIENCE?` · `I SEE NO GOOD IN KILLING MY KIN.` · `NO KINGDOM IS WORTH THEM.` · `THEY CAN'T SEE. WE CAN. TURN BACK.` · then, large: `HEARD IN FULL.`

segments.voice: Think of something in front of you that part of you really doesn't want to do, and first notice where your body tightens or goes cold. Then let the objection talk, fully, in its own words, the way Arjuna's does. Don't answer, argue or shame it; just listen to the end.
Gandiva, Arjuna's famous bow, slipping from his hand as his legs give way. Arjuna's case against the war: no victory, no kingdom, is worth the people he loves.

160.title: The yoga of despair
160.hook: the last argument, the last verse of chapter one, and a warrior sitting down in the middle of the field
160.carry: despair, too, is counted as a yoga
160.howItsDone: Chapter one of the Gita is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair; many readers and teachers treat Arjuna's collapse at 1.47 as the necessary starting point for the teaching that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandiva slipping from Arjuna's hand, and his case against the war, heard in full. Your line was doubt gets heard in full before it's answered. Today, the end of chapter one.

Some people know this moment. Weeks of holding it together, every argument made, to themselves and to everyone else. Then, one ordinary afternoon, in a parking lot or a kitchen or an office bathroom, they just sit down. Not because they decided to. Because they can't stand up anymore. That's where chapter one of the Gita ends. Not with a battle, but with the warrior Krishna drove into the middle of the field sitting down in his chariot, his bow on the floor.
screen: `WEEKS OF HOLDING IT TOGETHER.` → `ONE AFTERNOON, THEY SIT DOWN.` → `THE BOW ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Arjuna's last arguments, in verses forty to forty-four, are about what a war like this destroys beyond the dead. When a family is wiped out, he says, its old ways die with it: the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together. Chaos follows, and the generations after are lost. It's the argument of a man from his own time and world, and people read it differently today: some commentators hear real grief for everything a war erases, some hear a mind grabbing any argument it can find. Either way, it ends in a cry. Alas, he says, we're about to commit a great wrong, killing our own people out of greed for a kingdom. Then the line that's hardest to hear: it would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and not fighting back. And Sanjaya, telling the blind king, describes what he sees. In Sanskrit: visrijya sasharam chapam shoka samvigna manasah. Casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief, Arjuna sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, there between the two armies. That's the end of chapter one. And here's the surprise. Every chapter of the Gita has a title calling it a yoga, a path. This one is Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair. Despair, counted as a path. None of Krishna's teaching happens without this. The book begins because a man sat down and said, I can't.
screen: `WHAT A WAR ERASES.` · `BETTER IF THEY KILLED ME UNARMED.` · `HE CASTS ASIDE HIS BOW.` · `THE YOGA OF DESPAIR.` · then, large: `THE BOOK BEGINS WITH I CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been carrying and fighting with for too long, and picture it as a bow, heavy in your hands. Without deciding anything about tomorrow, set it down, let your hands be empty, and sit, the way Arjuna sits in his chariot. You don't have to fix anything yet. And if I can't ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number, today.
Vishada. Despair, dejection: the word that names chapter one, Arjuna Vishada Yoga. Arjuna casts aside his bow and arrows and sits down, his mind shaken with grief.
Your line: despair, too, is counted as a yoga. Tomorrow, Krishna answers him. Chapter one, all done.

161.title: I am your student
161.hook: Krishna's answer to a man in tears is not comfort; it's a jolt, and then Arjuna asks to be taught
161.carry: the teaching begins when you ask: teach me
161.tomorrow: The self that is not slain (2.11–2.25)
161.howItsDone: Commentators often treat Gita 2.7, where Arjuna says he is Krishna's student and asks to be taught, as the moment the teaching truly begins, and 2.3's call to cast off faintness and stand up is often quoted in times of discouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vishada: Arjuna sat down in his chariot, and chapter one ended on despair, too, is counted as a yoga. Your line was despair, too, is counted as a yoga. Today, Krishna answers.
screen: `DESPAIR, TOO, IS COUNTED AS A YOGA.`

segments.voice: Here's what kindness usually sounds like. A friend is on the floor in tears, saying I can't do this. Someone kneels, puts a hand on their back, and says: it's okay, you don't have to. Now here's Krishna, with his friend in exactly that state, in the middle of a battlefield. His first words are closer to: what is this? Where did this come from? Get up. Chapter two begins with a jolt.
screen: `A FRIEND ON THE FLOOR, IN TEARS.` → `IT'S OKAY, YOU DON'T HAVE TO.` → `KRISHNA SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya sets the scene: Arjuna, overcome with pity, eyes full of tears. He's already had one line from Krishna, look at them. Now come Krishna's first words of real answer. In Sanskrit: kutas tva kashmalam idam vishame samupasthitam. Older English translators rendered it something like, whence this dejection, at this hour of crisis? Then: klaibyam ma sma gamah Partha. Don't give in to this unmanly weakness. And: tyaktvottishtha parantapa. Cast off this petty faintness of heart and stand up, you who scorch your foes. It sounds harsh. But Krishna isn't agreeing with the story Arjuna tells about himself. He's reminding him who he is. And it doesn't work, not yet. Arjuna argues again. How can I shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, who deserve my worship? Better to live as a beggar. I don't even know which is better, winning or losing. Then the sentence that turns the whole book: shishyas te 'ham shadhi mam tvam prapannam. I am your student. Teach me. I've come to you for refuge. After that, he says, I will not fight, and he falls silent. And Krishna, between the two armies, answers him, the text says, as if smiling. The jolt wasn't the teaching. The jolt got Arjuna to ask. That's the shape of learning in Hinduism: the student comes to the teacher, the guru, and asks, and the Gita's whole teaching is given because Arjuna asked.
screen: `WHENCE THIS DEJECTION?` · `CAST IT OFF AND STAND UP.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `HE ANSWERS, AS IF SMILING.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING BEGINS WHEN YOU ASK.`

segments.voice: Go back to the bow you set down yesterday, the thing that's too much, and instead of I can't, try a different sentence: teach me how to face this. Say it inside, to God if you pray, or to life, or to your own wiser self. Then breathe, notice what changes in your body when you move from giving up to asking, and imagine someone answering, as if smiling.
Uttishtha. Stand up, arise — Krishna's call in Gita two, three. Where has this faintness come from, at this hour? Cast it off, and stand up.
Your line: the teaching begins when you ask: teach me. Tomorrow, Krishna starts teaching the one who asked. See you then.
